Shot density refers to the mass per unit volume of shotgun pellets, typically measured in grams per cubic centimeter (𝑔/𝑐𝑐), directly impacting energy retention, penetration, and effective range. Denser materials (e.g., TSS at 1 8𝑔/𝑐𝑐, lead at 1 1𝑔/𝑐𝑐) hit harder and carry energy longer than less dense options like steel (7.8𝑔/𝑐𝑐).[[1]](https://www.facebook.com/bossshotshells/posts/lets-talk-density-because-when-youre-out-there-chasing-late-season-birds-it-matt/639077662015858/)[[2]](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/dbUq5UyEDEQ)[[3]](https://www.nwtf.org/content-hub/turkey-load-pellet-science)

**Key Material Densities (approximate):** 

- **[Tungsten Super Shot](https://www.google.com/search?q=Tungsten+Super+Shot&csui=3&hl=en&gl=US&uule=w+CAIQIFISCQs2MuSEtepUEUK33kOSuTsc&ved=2ahUKEwjl2q6qlpGUAxVzA9sEHW-GEW4QgK4QegYIAQgAEA8) (TSS):** 1 8.1𝑔/𝑐𝑐
- **[HEVI-Shot](https://www.google.com/search?q=HEVI-Shot&csui=3&hl=en&gl=US&uule=w+CAIQIFISCQs2MuSEtepUEUK33kOSuTsc&ved=2ahUKEwjl2q6qlpGUAxVzA9sEHW-GEW4QgK4QegYIAQgAEBI) (Tungsten):** 1 2.0𝑔/𝑐𝑐
- **Lead:** 1 1.2𝑔/𝑐𝑐
- **Bismuth:** 9.6𝑔/𝑐𝑐
- **[Tungsten-Iron](https://www.google.com/search?q=Tungsten-Iron&csui=3&hl=en&gl=US&uule=w+CAIQIFISCQs2MuSEtepUEUK33kOSuTsc&ved=2ahUKEwjl2q6qlpGUAxVzA9sEHW-GEW4QgK4QegYIAQgCEAM):** 1 0.3𝑔/𝑐𝑐
- **Steel:** 7.8𝑔/𝑐𝑐[[1]](https://www.facebook.com/bossshotshells/posts/lets-talk-density-because-when-youre-out-there-chasing-late-season-birds-it-matt/639077662015858/)[[2]](https://apexmunition.com/learn-center/the-tss-difference/)[[3]](https://www.nwtf.org/content-hub/turkey-load-pellet-science)[[4]](https://www.federalpremium.com/its-federal-season/give-em-the-bismuth.html)[[5]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=27mBSKyHiFE#:~:text=Lead%20shot%20is%20the%20most%20dense%20at,is%20the%20least%20dense%20at%207.8%20g/cc.)

**Why Density Matters** 

- **Penetration & Energy:** Denser shot (like Tungsten or Lead) retains higher velocity downrange, leading to better penetration (deeper killing power).
- **Pattern Density:** Higher density materials allow for smaller shot sizes, which increases the number of pellets in a pattern while maintaining high energy, leading to better, tighter patterns.
- **Steel Limitations:** Due to its low density (7.8𝑔/𝑐𝑐), steel shot requires larger shot sizes to achieve similar downrange energy, which can lead to lower pellet counts (less dense patterns) compared to bismuth or lead.
- **Alternatives:** Bismuth (9.6𝑔/𝑐𝑐) offers a non-toxic, denser alternative to steel, acting more like lead with better penetration than steel.[[1]](https://www.facebook.com/bossshotshells/posts/lets-talk-density-because-when-youre-out-there-chasing-late-season-birds-it-matt/639077662015858/)[[2]](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/dbUq5UyEDEQ)[[3]](https://www.nwtf.org/content-hub/turkey-load-pellet-science)[[4]](https://apexmunition.com/learn-center/the-tss-difference/)[[5]](https://www.ducks.org/hunting/shooting-tips/kent-cartridge-guide-to-waterfowl-loads)[[6]](https://www.federalpremium.com/its-federal-season/give-em-the-bismuth.html)

**Key Concepts** 

- **[Pattern Density](https://www.google.com/search?q=Pattern+Density&csui=3&hl=en&gl=US&uule=w+CAIQIFISCQs2MuSEtepUEUK33kOSuTsc&ved=2ahUKEwjl2q6qlpGUAxVzA9sEHW-GEW4QgK4QegYIAQgBEBE):** The number of pellets that land inside a specific target area, not to be confused with the material density of the shot itself.
- **Velocity:** Often coupled with density on boxes, typically measured around 1,2 0 0--1,7 0 0 feet per second (fps) for hunting applications.[[1]](https://syrenusa.com/shotgun-pattern-density-vs-pellet-penetration/)[[2]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OWvUUXVt5pI&t=123)

references.title: Let’s talk density — because when you’re out there chasing late season birds, it matters. Steel? It’s got a density of about 7.8 g/cc. Not bad for shots inside 30 yards, but when you’re pushing range or dropping big birds, it can come up short. Enter bismuth, with a density of 9.6 g/cc. That’s serious stopping power, meaning tighter patterns, deeper penetration and fewer cripples to chase. We believe that sometimes the only way to do something right, is to do it yourself - and our manufacturing processes are the ultimate example. We don’t just source our bismuth pellets. We make them — in-house, from molten metal to round pellet. Our process starts with melting raw bismuth and tin to ensure the perfect alloy every time. Next, pouring our own shot pellets for consistent shape and weight. And finally, plating them with a layer of copper to boost performance. Delivering you ammunition that flies true, hits hard and gets the job done.
